title: The Red Child

zh.text: 含德之厚，比於赤子。蜂蠆虺蛇不螫，猛獸不據，攫鳥不搏。

gloss.3: thick, deep (as a layer of earth)
gloss.15: shì: to sting, to bite with poison
gloss.20: to seize and hold down (with paws)

gloss.5: to grip, to close the fist

gloss.7: whole; the silk texts are reported to read 朘, an infant’s penis

zh.text: 物壯則老，謂之不道，不道早已。

rendering: One who [[holds de within|han]], thick and deep,
[[Wasps, scorpions, vipers, snakes|du]] do not sting.
[[Bones weak, sinews soft|pair-soft-firm]], yet [[the grip is firm|wo-gu]].
Not yet knowing the joining of [[female and male|pinmu]],
[[Howls|hao]] all day and is not hoarse:
Knowing the constant is named clear sight.
Adding to life is named [[an omen|xiang]].
The heart-mind [[driving the breath|xin-shi-qi]] is named [[forcing|qiang]].
A thing in its prime [[then grows old|zhuang]].
What is not the Dao ends early.

han.title: 含: held in the mouth
han.body: 含 has 口, a mouth, at the bottom, and 今 above it for the sound. The Shuowen says 嗛也, “to hold in the mouth”. It is the verb for a thing kept behind closed lips and not swallowed and not spoken: a sweet, a sip of water, a word that is not said. So 含德 is not “to have virtue” as a person has a medal. It is 德 kept in, unshown, as a baby’s strength is all inside. 厚 is “thick”; the Shuowen explains it from the land, 山陵之厚也, “the thickness of hills”. The same verb named a funeral custom: a piece of jade, a 含, was put in the mouth of the dead. And the silk texts are reported to add 者 after 厚, which makes the subject plain: “the one who…”; our “one who” follows that, and our “thick and deep” is two words for the one word 厚. What do you hold in the mouth and not say?
src: Shuowen Jiezi, 口部: 含，嗛也。从口今聲。
Shuowen Jiezi, 㫗部: 厚，山陵之厚也。
Mawangdui silk texts, as printed in a modern collated edition (reported)

chizi.title: 赤子: why the child is red
chizi.body: 赤 is red: the Shuowen calls it 南方色也, “the colour of the south”, the colour of fire. 赤子, “red child”, is the newborn. The Tang scholar Yan Shigu gave the usual reason: a baby just born has no brows or hair yet, and its skin is red. 赤 also means “bare”: 赤手 is “bare-handed”, and to be 赤貧 is to be poor to the skin. So the word holds both facts of the first days: red, and with nothing on. English “infant” (Latin: one who cannot speak) and “baby” do not have this colour. The book returns to this figure often, as 嬰兒: in passage 10 (can you gather the breath, be soft, be an infant?), in passage 20 (like an infant that has not yet smiled), in passage 28 (return to the infant). Mencius knew the image too: the great person is one who has not lost 赤子之心, the heart of the red child.
src: Shuowen Jiezi, 赤部: 赤，南方色也。从大从火。
Yan Shigu, commentary on the Hanshu, “Jia Yi zhuan” (賈誼傳)
Mencius 4B12

du.title: Why nothing stings: Wang Bi
du.body: Is the infant protected by magic? Later religion sometimes read the lines so, and passage 50 has a like claim about the rhinoceros and the tiger. Wang Bi’s answer is plain: 赤子無求無欲，不犯眾物，故毒蟲之物無犯之人也. “The red child seeks nothing and desires nothing, and does not trespass on the many things; so the creatures with poison do not trespass on such a person.” The verb is 犯, to cross a line, to offend. Animals strike what threatens or what flees. The baby does neither. The line is not a claim that a baby cannot be bitten. It is a picture of a being with no aggression in it for another aggression to meet. He goes on: 含德之厚者，不犯於物，故無物以損其全也, “one who holds de thickly does not trespass on things, so nothing has a way to harm their wholeness”. The silk texts and the Guodian slips are reported to have two clauses where we have three: 蜂蠆虺蛇弗螫，攫鳥猛獸弗搏, with no 不據.
src: Wang Bi commentary on Laozi 55

wo-gu.title: 握固: the baby’s fist
wo-gu.body: Put a finger in a newborn’s palm and the hand shuts on it, hard. Doctors call it the grasp reflex. The text saw it 2,300 years ago and saw the paradox: the bones are weak, the sinews soft, and the grip is 固. The Shuowen defines 固 as 四塞也, “shut on four sides”: the character is a wall 囗 around its sound-part 古. The strength of the hold does not come from hard muscle. It comes from a hand with no doubt in it. The Zhuangzi quotes a version of these lines and adds: 終日握而手不掜, “it grips all day and the hand does not cramp”. Later Daoist breathing manuals made 握固 a technical term: a fist with the thumb folded inside under the four fingers, as a baby holds it, used in sitting practice to “keep the breath in”. Try it for a minute. Is it effort?
src: Shuowen Jiezi, 囗部: 固，四塞也。从囗古聲。
Zhuangzi, “Gengsang Chu” (庚桑楚)

pinmu.title: 牝牡: words from the stable
pinmu.body: The text does not say 男女, “man and woman”. It says 牝牡, and both characters have 牛, an ox, at the left. The Shuowen defines them as 畜母也 and 畜父也: “the mother among livestock”, “the father among livestock”. These are a herdsman’s words for cow and bull, mare and stallion. 合 is “to join”, and for animals it is the plain word for mating. So the line speaks of sex as a farmer does, without shame and without romance. English versions move it up a register: “the union of male and female”, “the union of the sexes”. The Chinese stays in the yard. 牝 is also one of the great words of this book: the dark female of passage 6, and the female that wins by stillness in passage 61. Here the infant is before all that, before two.
src: Shuowen Jiezi, 牛部: 牝，畜母也。从牛匕聲。
Shuowen Jiezi, 牛部: 牡，畜父也。从牛土聲。

quan-zuo.title: 全作: what the scribes covered
quan-zuo.body: Our text says 全作, “the whole rises”, and we wrote “fully roused”. It is an odd phrase, and the older texts show why. The silk texts are reported to read 未知牝牡之合而朘怒. 朘 (zuī) is a baby boy’s penis (the Shuowen has the character 脧: 赤子陰也, “the sex of a red child”), and 怒 is “to swell with force”, the word for anger and also for a bud that bursts or a river in flood. So: “with no knowledge yet of how female and male join, its small member stands”. An erection with no desire and no object: the text points at it as proof that the life-force is full when the mind wants nothing. Some received editions are reported to keep 朘作 or 峻作. Wang Bi’s text already had 全, and he explains it with care: 作，長也, “作 is to grow”; nothing harms the body, so it can 全長, “grow whole”. A rare character was lost, or a blunt one was made polite. [[Legge|legge]] made it more polite still.
src: Mawangdui silk texts, as printed in a modern collated edition (reported)
Wang Bi commentary on Laozi 55

jing.title: 精: the picked grain
jing.body: 精 has 米, husked grain, at the left; 青 gives the sound. The Shuowen says only 擇也, “to select”: grain that has been picked over and polished, the best of the crop. From “the finest part” the word went to the finest part of anything: of a metal, of the breath, of a body. In the body 精 is the stuff of life at its most dense, and in particular it is semen. That is why this line follows the one before it. English “essence” has lost the body; it sounds like perfume or philosophy. “Vitality” has no substance in it. 精 is a thing that a person has in a certain amount and can spend. Texts of the same age, such as the “Inward Training” in the Guanzi, tell the student how to store it. Later it became the first of three “treasures”, with [[氣|xin-shi-qi]] and 神, spirit.
src: Shuowen Jiezi, 米部: 精，擇也。从米青聲。
Guanzi, “Nei ye” (內業)

hao.title: 號: a cry that does not hurt
hao.body: 號 here is read háo: to howl, to wail. An adult who shouts for an hour is hoarse the next day. A baby can cry from morning to night and its voice is as strong at the end. Why? The adult shouts from the throat, against a tight chest, with a purpose and with fear of how it sounds. The baby cries with the whole belly, and nothing in it resists the cry. The text names this 和之至, [[harmony|he]] at its peak: sound that does not fight its own body. The Zhuangzi gives the same line with a small change: 終日嗥而嗌不嗄, “it howls all day and its throat is not hoarse”. Watch a baby breathe if you can. The belly moves, and the shoulders do not. Then put a hand on your own belly and say one long “ah”. Where does it start?
src: Zhuangzi, “Gengsang Chu”

he.title: 和: not peace and quiet
he.body: The proof of 和 in this passage is a baby that screams all day. That should stop us if we hear “harmony” as calm, niceness, or the lack of conflict. 和 has 口, a mouth; the Shuowen says 相譍也, “to answer one another”, as voices do in a song. Early texts explain it from music and from the kitchen: different notes that answer, different tastes that blend in a broth. A cook does not get 和 with one taste. So 和 is a fit between parts that are different and all active. In the infant the parts are breath, voice, belly, and want, and they act as one. Passage 42 says where this comes from: the ten thousand things carry yin and hold yang, and 沖氣以為和, the breaths blend and make 和. Can a loud thing be in harmony? Can a quiet thing be out of it?
src: Shuowen Jiezi, 口部: 和，相譍也。从口禾聲。

chang.title: 常 and 明: a chain with a missing link
chang.body: 知常曰明, “knowing the constant is named clear sight”, also stands in passage 16, where the constant is the return of each thing to its root. Here a step is put before it: 知和曰常, “knowing harmony is named the constant”. The silk texts are reported to be shorter: 和曰常，知和曰明, “harmony is named the constant; knowing harmony is named clear sight”. That is cleaner logic, and it has no “knowing the constant” at all; the received text was perhaps made to match passage 16. Where we have 常, older copies often have 恆; it was changed under a Han emperor’s name taboo. Wang Bi describes the constant as a temperature: 不皦不昧，不溫不涼，此常也, “not glaring, not dim, not warm, not cool: this is the constant”. 明 is 日 and 月, sun and moon, in its modern form. It is the light that sees, not cleverness.
src: Mawangdui silk texts, as printed in a modern collated edition (reported)
Wang Bi commentary on Laozi 55

xiang.title: 祥: a blessing that is a warning
xiang.body: This line and the next can be read as praise: “to increase life is auspicious; the mind that commands the breath is strong”. 祥 does usually mean a good sign, and it is on New Year cards today; the Shuowen, a Han book, gives only that sense: 福也, “a blessing”. But the word is first a neutral one: any sign from heaven or earth. In the Zuozhuan a duke sees meteors fall and asks: 是何祥也，吉凶焉在, “what omen is this? Where is the good or ill fortune in it?” The old commentators all take it as an ill omen here, and the grammar agrees: these two lines lead straight to “a thing in its prime then grows old”. Wang Bi: 生不可益，益之則夭也, “life cannot be added to; add to it and you die young”. 益 is the picture of water over the brim of a dish. Life is full already. Tonics, regimens, ambition for more years: the text calls the wish itself a sign.
src: Zuozhuan, Xi 16
Wang Bi commentary on Laozi 55
Shuowen Jiezi, 皿部: 益，饒也。从水、皿。皿，益之意也。

xin-shi-qi.title: 心使氣: against Mencius
xin-shi-qi.body: 心 is the heart, and in Chinese the heart thinks: “heart-mind”. 氣 is breath, and also the energy that moves in a living body. 使 is to give orders, as a lord sends a servant. So 心使氣 is the mind in command of the breath and the energy: will-power. Mencius, in the same century, praised exactly this. 夫志，氣之帥也, he says: “the will is the general of the 氣”, and he was proud of his own “flood-like 氣”, fed by right action. The Laozi puts the general under suspicion. Wang Bi: 心宜無有，使氣則強, “the heart should have nothing in it; if it drives the breath, that is forcing”. This is a real quarrel between two schools about the body: do you train it by command, or by removing the commander? The baby is the Laozi’s evidence. Its breath is perfect and nobody is in charge of it.
src: Mencius 2A2
Wang Bi commentary on Laozi 55

qiang.title: 強: one word, two values
qiang.body: 強 is “strong”, and the book uses it both ways. Passage 33: one who overcomes the self is 強. Passage 52: to keep to the soft is called 強. Those are praise. But passage 30 says: get the result and do not 強, do not force. Passage 42: the violent and 強 do not die a natural death. Passage 76: the hard and 強 are the companions of death. Here the form of the line, “X is called 強”, is the same as in passage 52, and only the content shows that the value has turned. English must pick “strength” or “forcing” and so hide the pun. A fact for the curious: the Shuowen defines the character 強 as an insect, 蚚也, a grain weevil; it has 虫 in it. The proper character for “strong” was 彊, which has a bow, 弓: 弓有力也, “a bow that has power”. Scribes borrowed the weevil.
src: Shuowen Jiezi, 虫部: 強，蚚也。从虫弘聲。
Shuowen Jiezi, 弓部: 彊，弓有力也。从弓畺聲。

zhuang.title: 物壯則老: the same lines, a new place
zhuang.body: The last three lines are also the last three lines of passage 30. There the subject is war: do not use arms to force the realm, for a campaign at its height is close to its fall. Here the same words close a passage about a baby. 壯 is the full strength of an adult; the ritual books give it an age, 三十曰壯, “at thirty one is called 壯”. So the passage sets two bodies side by side. The infant: weak bones, and all its life ahead. The man of thirty at his peak: and the next word is 老, old. To push toward the peak is to push toward the far side of it. That is why it is 不道, “not the Dao”. Was the saying moved here from passage 30, or was it a proverb that both drew on? We do not know. Does it change when the subject is your own body and not an army?
src: Liji, “Quli”: 三十曰壯，有室。

legge.title: Legge’s Latin moment
legge.body: Legge was a Victorian missionary, and this passage tested him. For the infant’s body he finds the phrase “its virile member may be excited”: Latin words, a passive verb, and “may”. In truth his text only had 全作; the commentaries supplied the anatomy, and he followed them honestly. For 精 he writes “physical essence”, and for 德 “the attributes (of the Tao)”: a term from Christian theology, where God has attributes. Then he turns the four sayings into a rhymed stanza with a “throne” for wisdom, and ends on a line that is almost all brackets: “(False) is the strength, (and o’er it we should mourn.)” Only three words of that are in the Chinese: 曰強, “is called 強”. He read the sense correctly, as a warning. But count the words that he needed to make a warning sound like one.
src: James Legge, The Texts of Taoism, Sacred Books of the East vol. 39 (1891)

alchemy.title: What later Daoists did with the baby
alchemy.body: This passage became a charter for the arts of long life. Its words are their vocabulary: [[精|jing]], 氣, 和, [[握固|wo-gu]]. From the Han onward, teachers of breathing and “guiding and pulling” exercises told students to breathe like an infant, low and soft. Inner alchemy, from the Tang and Song, went further and spoke of an “infant” that the adept forms inside the body by refining 精 into 氣 and 氣 into spirit. There is an irony, and the tradition knew it. The passage also says 益生曰祥: to [[add to life is an ill omen|xiang]]. A school of life-extension took its texts from a passage that warns against the wish to extend life. The better teachers answered that the work is to stop spending, not to add. Is there a difference between care for life and greed for it? Where is the line in you?

pair-soft-firm.title: 弱 / 固: weak bones, firm grip
pair-soft-firm.body: The line sets 弱 and 柔, weak and soft, beside 固, firm, and joins them with 而. That small word is “and” as much as “yet”; our “yet” leans on the surprise. In the infant the two are not at war. The grip is firm because nothing in the hand works against it. The passage then gives a second pair, 壯 and 老, [[prime and old age|zhuang]], and there one side becomes the other in three characters. The text does favour the soft and the young. The favour is a correction, to an age and to a reader that push toward the peak. It is not a rule that weak is good. The infant’s softness also turns: the child grows. And [[強|qiang]] is a word of praise in other passages. A one-sided reading would have you act weak. The text shows a state in which soft and firm have not yet come apart.

lenses.ground: A newborn is described as a naturalist would describe it, by four facts. Animals do not attack it. Its bones are soft and [[its fist is tight|wo-gu]]. It knows nothing of sex and [[its body rises|quan-zuo]]. It [[howls all day|hao]] and is not hoarse. After the third fact comes a verdict: [[精|jing]] at its peak. After the fourth: [[和|he]] at its peak. Then four short definitions in the form “X is called Y”, two that praise and two that warn, and the warning is easy to miss because [[祥|xiang]] and [[強|qiang]] look like good words. Then a proverb that also ends passage 30. The first line says that all this is a likeness: the person who [[holds 德 within|han]] is “like” the [[red child|chizi]]. It does not say “is” one.
lenses.inner: The infant is not innocent in a moral sense, and the text does not say it is good. It is undivided. It has no second self that watches the first, so its grip has no doubt in it and its cry has no shame in it. Each of the four facts is strength without a one who is strong. Then the text names the adult disease with precision: [[心使氣|xin-shi-qi]], the mind that takes command of the breath. The return to the infant is not a return to ignorance. A grown person cannot un-know. What can stop is the constant small act of command: the held belly, the managed face, the life that is [[added to|xiang]]. The text calls what is left 和, and to know it, 常. Notice that the infant has 和 and does not know it. Only the adult can “know harmony”.
lenses.leading: Read the animals as politics for a moment. Wasps, vipers, beasts, and raptors are what a court is made of. [[Wang Bi|du]] gives the rule: the one who does not trespass is not trespassed on. A person with no hidden aim offers nothing for an attack to hold. This is not a method to act harmless; a grown predator smells an act. The second half is for any organization. [[壯|zhuang]], the peak year, the record quarter, the largest army, is the point at which age starts. A leader who drives the body of the group by will, [[心使氣|xin-shi-qi]], gets force for a time and then an early end: 早已. The rulers of the time called their subjects 赤子 and promised to guard them like babies. The Laozi turns it round: the ruler should be like the baby.
lenses.body: This is the book’s passage on the body. Take its claims as instructions for the hands, belly, and voice. Hands: soft bones, firm grip. In the arts of the sword, the brush, and the bow, teachers say the same: hold it as you would hold a small bird, fully, with no squeeze. Belly: the breath of a baby moves low and nothing pulls it. Voice: sound from the belly does not tear the throat. Then the warning. [[心使氣|xin-shi-qi]] is the athlete’s error: to push the breath, to grit through. It works, and it costs. Many students of taijiquan hear a rule that comes from this line: use intent, do not use force, and do not drive the 氣. [[精|jing]] is not made by effort. It is what remains when it is not wasted. See what [[later schools|alchemy]] built on this.
lenses.nature: Young things are soft. A shoot bends where the old branch cracks; passage 76 says it outright: the living are soft and weak, the dead hard and strong. A seedling has all the growth of the tree still in it, and in that sense the smallest form holds the most life. The curve that the last lines draw is the curve of every living thing: rise, [[peak|zhuang]], decline. The text does not say that the curve can be escaped. It says that to rush toward the peak is 不道, and that what does so ends early. A fruit tree forced to bear heavily for a few years is spent. The old growers thinned the fruit. [[To add to life|xiang]] is to take from it.
lenses.practice: Today, three times, drop the general. Stop where you are, put a hand low on the belly, and for five breaths give the breath no orders: not slow, not deep, not “right”. Let it be short or rough if it is. See how hard it is to watch a breath and not manage it. That small urge to manage is [[心使氣|xin-shi-qi]]. Then try the [[baby’s fist|wo-gu]] and the [[long “ah”|hao]]. Do not make a regimen of this. A regimen is [[益生|xiang]].

plates.title: A person over a fire
plates.lesson: The Shuowen takes this character apart in four words: 从大从火, “from 大 and from 火”. 大 is “big”, and the dictionary says that it is the shape of a human being: 天大，地大，人亦大。故大象人形, “heaven is great, earth is great, and the human is also great; so 大 shows a person’s form”. (That first phrase is a quotation from passage 25 of this book.) 火 is fire, a picture of flames. So 赤 is a person above a fire, or a great fire: the red of flame, the colour of the south and of summer. In the modern shape both parts are hard to see. The top has become a form like 土, and the fire below has opened into four strokes. A cousin makes it plain: 赫, “blazing, awesome”, is two 赤 side by side, and the Shuowen calls it 火赤皃, “the look of fire-red”. Chinese has several reds. 朱 is vermilion. 丹 is cinnabar, the red mineral of the alchemists. 紅, the usual word today, has the silk radical and was first a pale dyed red. 赤 is the oldest and the barest, and it also means bare: 赤手, bare-handed. A [[red child|chizi]] is a person with nothing on and nothing added, still warm from the fire.
plates.brush: Seven strokes. A short horizontal; a short vertical that crosses it; then a long horizontal, the widest line of the character. Those three are what is left of the person. Then the fire: a stroke that goes down and curves away to the left; a vertical with a hook; a dot on the left side that falls leftward; a dot on the right. Watch strokes four and five. They are the two legs of the form and they must stand apart under the long horizontal like the legs of a stool, with the two dots outside them like sparks. In seal script the person and the flames are still clear, one above the other. In running script the four lower strokes are often written in one turning movement, and the fire seems to flicker.

plates.title: Vapour, and a gift of rice
plates.lesson: Two parts: 气 above and around, 米 inside. Start with 气. The Shuowen: 雲气也。象形, “cloud vapour; a picture”. Its early form is widely explained as three thin level lines, a picture of mist or cloud layers; to keep it apart from the number 三, the top line was bent up and the bottom line bent down, and that is the hook you see today. That was the first way to write “vapour, breath”. 米 is grain: the Shuowen calls it 象禾實之形, a picture of the seeds of the crop. Now the surprise. The Shuowen does not define 氣 as breath at all. It says 饋客芻米也, “fodder and grain that are presented to a guest”. 氣 was the character for a gift of provisions, a word now written 餼. Scribes then borrowed the fuller character for “breath”, and the plain 气 fell out of use for two thousand years, until the simplified script brought it back. People love to read 氣 as steam that rises from cooking rice, and as a memory aid it is perfect: breath is what food becomes. But it is a later reading of a loan. Later Daoists used a third character, 炁, for the breath that a person has before birth. In this passage 氣 is what the baby has in full and [[the mind, when it drives it, is said to force|xin-shi-qi]].
plates.brush: Ten strokes. First 气, four strokes: a short stroke that falls to the left; a horizontal; a second, shorter horizontal; then the great stroke of the character, which goes right, turns, sweeps down in a long curve to the lower right, and ends with a hook upward. Watch this fourth stroke. It makes a roof and a wall at once, and it must leave a room under it. Then 米 goes into that room, six strokes: a dot at upper left, a dot at upper right that leans inward, a horizontal, a vertical through it, then a stroke that falls to the left and one that falls to the right. The grain should sit low and left, sheltered, and not touch the curve. In cursive hands the long hook is thrown out in one breath. Calligraphers use this very word for the life of a line: a stroke has 氣 or it is dead.

plates.title: A cry with a tiger in it
plates.lesson: The baby [[howls|hao]], and the character for the howl has a tiger in it. On the left is 号. The Shuowen gives it an entry of its own: 痛聲也。从口在丂上, “the sound of pain; a mouth 口 above 丂”, where 丂 is commonly explained as breath that tries to come out and is blocked. On the right is 虎, the tiger, 山獸之君, “lord of the mountain beasts”. The dictionary joins them without comment: 號，呼也。从号从虎, “to call out; from 号 and 虎”. So a cry of pain plus the roar of the largest animal that a Chinese farmer could meet: a full-throated howl. The word then widened. To cry out a thing is to proclaim it, so 號 (read hào) came to mean an order, a signal, a title, a name that is called out, and at last a number: the modern 三號 is “number three”. The simplified script kept only the left half, 号. 虎 as a part gives its top, 虍, to other characters: 虐 (cruel), 慮 (to worry), 處 (to dwell). The passage chose the wild word on purpose. This is not the baby’s “voice”. It is the tiger in a body with soft bones, and it does not go hoarse.
plates.brush: Thirteen strokes. The left side takes five: the mouth in three (a vertical; a horizontal that turns down; a closing horizontal), then a horizontal below it, then one stroke that goes down, bends, and ends in a hook to the left. The right side, the tiger, takes eight. A short vertical and a short horizontal at the top. A horizontal that ends in a hook, like a brow. A long stroke that falls to the left: the tiger’s back, and the longest line of the character. A short horizontal and a bent stroke with a hook inside. Then the two legs: a stroke that falls to the left, and a last stroke that goes down, turns right, and hooks up. The left half is small and held high; the tiger is tall and takes the weight. The two final hooks, one in each half, turn away from each other.

questions.claim: What is pushed to its peak grows old early.
prompts: Do you believe it? Where have you seen a person, a team, or a body reach its height and then fall fast?
What in your past taught you to push for the peak? Was there praise for it, or a fear of being ordinary?
Now take the other side: a life held back from its peak is a life not lived, and it is right to burn. Say it as your own belief for a few minutes. What feelings come with it?
Which of the two do you hear as wisdom and which as an excuse? What would someone who knows you well say?

questions.claim: The effort to add to life, and to drive the breath by will, is a strain and not a strength.
prompts: Does that match your experience of effort, training, and self-improvement?
Think of one regimen that you keep. What does it promise to protect you from?
Hold the opposite for a while: nothing good comes without will, and the body left to itself goes slack. What do you notice as you hold it: agreement, tiredness, pride?
The infant in the passage has harmony and does not know it. Do you trust anything in yourself that you did not make by effort? If not, when did that trust go?
Why might it matter which of these two views runs your day?
